title: Which word is it? a chain of matches
idea: Use if/elif/else to react differently to each of several possible words. Predict which branch a given word triggers.

exercises.prompt: To react differently to "red", "green", or "yellow", the natural structure is...
options: if color == "red" ... elif color == "green" ... elif color == "yellow" ... else
exercises.explanation: Each word gets its own branch in an if/elif chain, with else catching anything unexpected.
"green" fails the red test but matches the green elif, so "Go" prints.
"blue" matches neither named branch, so the else catches it: "Wait".

exercises.prompt: Why is the else branch important here?
options: It handles any word you did not expect, so the program always responds
exercises.explanation: Users can type anything. The else is a safety net for words outside your known list.

exercises.prompt: Arrange a command handler: "go" prints "Moving", "stop" prints "Halting", anything else prints "Unknown".
exercises.explanation: One branch per command, else for anything unrecognized. The chain reacts to which word it got.

exercises.prompt:
Fill the keyword so the "stop" test only runs if "go" did not match:

if cmd == "go":
    print("Moving")
____ cmd == "stop":
    print("Halting")
exercises.explanation: 'elif' chains the next word test, running only when the earlier one failed.

exercises.prompt: For the command handler, cmd = "stop" prints...
exercises.explanation: "stop" fails the "go" test but matches the "stop" elif, so "Halting" prints.

exercises.prompt: An if/elif chain on words stops at the first word that matches.
exercises.explanation: Yes - like any if/elif chain, the first true branch runs and the rest are skipped. Only one message appears.

exercises.prompt: If two branches test the same word, which runs?
options: Only the first one - the chain stops there
exercises.explanation: The chain stops at the first match, so a duplicate later branch is unreachable - a sign to clean up the logic.

options: Chain word tests with if/elif/else to react to each possible word, else for the rest
exercises.explanation: A word menu maps cleanly onto an if/elif/else chain, with else as the catch-all. That is how programs read commands.
